dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Kit had made it as far as the kitchen doorway before Bear moved, which was further than usual and had clearly been allowed.

"You let me get that far," Kit said, backing up one step.

"I did," Bear agreed. "I'm feeling generous."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: "Don't be," I say, and go.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear's laugh followed Kit out of the room, low and warm. He counted to four in his head — a deliberate, generous four — before pushing off from the counter.

His footsteps were unhurried through the living room, heavy enough that Kit would hear them coming. He rounded the corner into the hallway and paused, listening. The house settled around him, creaking in all its familiar places. He knew where Kit liked to hide, which corners gave the best advantage, which doorways squeaked.

"Four seconds," he called out, voice carrying easily. "That's a good head start. You should've taken the kitchen. Better exits."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I slide into the half-open closet under the stairs, holding my breath. "Kitchen's too obvious," I call back, my voice muffled by coats.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear stopped just past the hallway, letting the silence stretch. He could see the closet door from where he stood — slightly ajar, the way it always hung when someone had recently pushed past the coats.

"Under the stairs," he said, not moving. "Bold choice. Tight quarters. No easy exit if I find you."

He took a step, then another, his boots deliberate on the hardwood. When he reached the closet door, he didn't open it — just stood there, close enough that his shadow fell across the gap.

"Cozy in there?"

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: He catches me in the hallway, which was always going to happen, and I don't put much into getting away.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear reached out and caught the closet door, pulling it open the rest of the way. Kit was pressed back among the coats, not exactly cowering, but not looking like he was about to bolt either.

Bear braced one arm against the doorframe and leaned in, filling the space with his shoulders.

"Hallway," he repeated, voice dropping low. "You had the whole house and you picked the one spot I checked first. Every time."

He reached in and hooked a finger through one of Kit's belt loops, tugging him forward out of the coats.

"You're not even breathing hard." Bear's thumb brushed the jut of Kit's hip. "Should I be offended, or did you just want me to catch you?"

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I grin up at him, leaning into the pull. "Maybe I just like it when you look smug."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear's grin widened at that, slow and sharp. He gave the belt loop a tug that brought Kit flush against him, one hand sliding up to curl around the back of his neck.

"Smug looks are earned," he murmured, thumb brushing the hinge of Kit's jaw. "And you just handed me the win without breaking a sweat. That's not a chase, that's a participation trophy."

He held Kit there a beat, close enough to feel the warmth of him, before easing back just enough to meet his eyes.

"Unless you want a rematch. I'll give you five seconds this time. Real head start. You might actually work up a sweat."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: We don't make it to the bedroom. The floor is fine. Clothes are a problem we solve badly and fast.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear didn't need the invitation twice. The belt loop was still in his grip, and he used it to pull Kit off balance, walking him backward until Kit's shoulders hit the hallway wall. The coats swayed from the disturbance, a few slipping off their hangers.

"Floor's cold," Bear said, but he was already dropping to his knees, hands finding Kit's hips and dragging him down to meet him. The rest of the sentence was lost against Kit's mouth, or maybe just lost.

Clothes became a tangle of fabric and laughter and low, bitten-off sounds. Bear got Kit's shirt rucked up to his collarbone and paused just long enough to run his mouth over the strip of bare stomach, teeth scraping.

"Should've taken the kitchen," he murmured against warm skin. "Better floor for this. But I'm not complaining."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I shove his shirt up too, fingers digging into his shoulders. "Shut up," I say, breathless, and kiss him again.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear's laugh was a low rumble against Kit's mouth, and he answered the kiss with teeth, catching Kit's lower lip between his own and tugging just hard enough to sting.

"Make me," he breathed, the challenge rough in his throat.

His hands found Kit's hips again, dragging him forward off the wall and onto the floor. The impact was a solid thud, and Bear followed him down, bracing himself on forearms that caged Kit in. The hardwood was hard and cold against his knees, against Kit's back, but Bear didn't give either of them time to think about it.

He dipped his head, mouth finding the hinge of Kit's jaw, then lower, tongue tracing the line of his throat before teeth pressed in — not hard enough to mark, just enough to promise. His voice came out roughened, a little pleased.

"Five seconds next time. Maybe you'll actually make me work for it."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: He gets his teeth into my shoulder hard enough to leave something and I tell him to do it again, and he does.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear's teeth found the same spot, then dragged lower to sink into the curve where Kit's neck met his shoulder. He held it there, feeling the sharp inhale against his mouth, the way Kit's body arched up into his. When he pulled back, the mark was dark and already blooming.

"There," Bear said, voice rough, thumb brushing over the fresh bite. "That's the one you'll feel tomorrow."

His hand slid down Kit's side, grip tightening on his thigh to pull him in closer. The floor was unforgiving beneath them, but Bear didn't seem to notice. He ducked his head again, mouthing at the edge of the mark, tongue flat against the heat of it.

"Say it again," he murmured. "Tell me what you want and I'll give it to you."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: "Harder," I breathe out, my head tipping back against the floor. "And move."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear's breath caught at the word, low and rough in his throat. He pulled back just enough to look down at Kit — flushed, marked, head tipped back against the hardwood. The sight of him like that, demanding, did something hot and immediate low in Bear's gut.

"Yeah?" Bear's voice had gone gravel. "You want harder? You want me to leave you something you'll feel every time you move?"

He shifted, settling more heavily against Kit, one hand sliding down to grip his thigh and hook it up over his hip. The position pulled them flush together, and Bear held himself there a breath, letting the weight of the question hang.

"Ask me nice," he murmured, mouth brushing the shell of Kit's ear. "And I'll give you everything."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: "Marks," I tell him. "I want to find them in the mirror tomorrow and I want them to still hurt on Thursday." I put my wrists where he can reach them.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear's breath stuttered out of him at the words, at the offered wrists, at the raw honesty of the demand. He looked at Kit for a long moment — flushed, marked, wrists raised — and something in his chest went tight and hot all at once.

"Yeah," he said, voice gone rough. "Yeah, okay."

He caught Kit's wrists in one hand, pinning them above his head against the floor. The other hand came up to cup his jaw, tilting his head to the side to bare the already-bruising mark on his shoulder. Bear leaned down and pressed his mouth to it — not teeth this time, just the flat of his tongue, a slow drag that made the point clear.

"Thursday," he murmured against the skin. "I want you to feel this every time you move. Every time you reach for something, stretch, breathe." He shifted his weight, settling heavier against Kit, and his voice dropped lower. "And I want you to remember exactly how you asked for it."

He lifted his head just enough to meet Kit's eyes, pupils blown dark.

"You still want to tell me what you need? Or do you trust me to figure it out?"

He didn't wait for an answer — just lowered his mouth to the other side of Kit's throat and bit down, hard enough to leave a promise, working the skin between his teeth until he was satisfied. When he pulled back, there was a matching mark already darkening.

"One for each hand," he murmured, releasing Kit's wrists to brace himself above him. "Now tell me where you want the rest."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I arch up against him, gasping. "Anywhere you want them. I don't care."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear's breath came out in a low, approving hum at the words. He shifted his grip, one hand sliding down Kit's side to grip his hip, fingers pressing into the meat of it hard enough to leave bruises that would bloom later.

"That's what I thought," he murmured against Kit's skin, mouth trailing down over his collarbone, teeth scraping over the jut of bone before sinking in. He worked the spot until he was satisfied, then moved lower, tongue tracing the line of his chest, teeth finding a nipple and worrying it just enough to draw a sharp inhale.

He lifted his head just enough to meet Kit's eyes, his own dark and heavy-lidded. "You're going to be a map by the time I'm done with you." His hand slid lower, fingers splaying over Kit's stomach, pressing flat. "And I'm going to enjoy every single mark I leave."

He lowered his mouth to the opposite side of Kit's chest, teeth finding purchase just below the collarbone, and bit down with deliberate, patient pressure. When he pulled back, the mark was deep and already darkening, ringed with the imprint of his teeth.

"One," he said, voice rough. "Count them if you want. I've got all night."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I've stopped keeping score and so has he. "Don't stop," I tell him. (OOC: no fade, no skip -- write the whole thing.)

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear let the words hang there for a moment, the heat of Kit's "don't stop" still settling between them. He pulled back just enough to look down at the work he'd already done — the darkening marks on Kit's neck, his collarbone, the one just below his chest. A map, he'd called it. He intended to finish the cartography.

"Wasn't planning on it," he said, voice rough, and lowered his mouth again.

He took his time. There was no rush now, no chase left to run — just the two of them on the cold hallway floor, Kit's body opening under his hands like he had all the time in the world. Bear worked his way down the center of Kit's chest, tongue dragging over the line of his sternum, teeth scraping over each rib in turn. He left a mark on the jut of one hip bone, then the other, biting down hard enough to bruise, soothed by the flat of his tongue until Kit's breath came in uneven stutters.

"You feel that?" Bear murmured against the hollow of Kit's hip, mouthing at the skin there. "That one's going to ache every time you sit down tomorrow. I want you thinking about me every time you shift in your chair."

His hands slid up Kit's thighs, pushing them apart, settling his own weight between. He lifted his head just long enough to meet Kit's eyes, pupils blown wide, lips red from use.

"Still with me?" He didn't need to ask — he could feel it in the way Kit moved under him, the way his hands fisted in the floor — but he wanted to hear it. "Tell me you're still with me."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: "Yeah," I gasp, my fingers curling into his hair. "Right here."

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear's breath caught at the words, at the fingers curling into his hair, at the raw immediacy of Kit's voice. He turned his head just enough to press his mouth to the inside of Kit's wrist — the pulse point, where he could feel the wild beat of it — and held there a moment, eyes closed.

"Good," he said, voice rough and low. "Keep saying that. Keep telling me you're here."

He lifted his head, meeting Kit's eyes, and then he moved — shifting down, hands sliding under Kit's thighs to hook them over his shoulders. He pressed a kiss to the inside of one thigh, then the other, teeth dragging over the sensitive skin there before he bit down, hard enough to leave a mark that would darken and ache for days.

"That one's for Thursday," he murmured against the skin, mouthing over the fresh bite. "And this one's for me."

He bit down on the other thigh, higher up, closer to where Kit would feel it every time he moved, and worked the skin between his teeth until he was satisfied. When he pulled back, both thighs bore his marks, dark and blooming against the pale skin.

"Look at you," he breathed, voice thick with something like awe. "Spread out on my floor, marked up, telling me not to stop." He dragged his hands up Kit's thighs, over his hips, settling his weight back over him. "You have no idea what you do to me."

He leaned down, mouth brushing Kit's ear, voice dropping to a low rasp.

"Now I'm going to take you apart slow. And I'm not going to stop until you can't remember your own name."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: I laugh, breathless and strained. "You already know my name." I hook my ankle around his calf and pull.

dialogue.name: Bear
dialogue.content:
Bear's laugh was a low, warm rumble against Kit's skin, and he let the ankle hook pull him down, settling his weight back over him with a deliberate roll of his hips.

"Fair point," he murmured, mouth trailing up the line of Kit's throat, teeth grazing his jaw. "I know your name. I know the sound you make when you mean it and the one you make when you're lying." His hand slid down Kit's side, fingers pressing into his hip. "I know the spot on your neck that makes you go quiet, and the one that makes you loud."

He lifted his head just enough to meet Kit's eyes, his own dark and heavy-lidded.

"But I want to hear you say it. Right now, like this, while I've got you spread out on my floor with my marks on your skin." His thumb brushed over the bruise on Kit's hip, feather-light. "Tell me your name. And tell me you're not going anywhere."

dialogue.name: Kit
dialogue.content: "Kit," I say, my voice shaky. "And I'm not going anywhere you don't come with me."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
The room was set up the way it always was before a scene, which Ari found steadying: everything in its place, nothing improvised.

Vex checked the last strap without hurrying. "Colour," she said. It was not a question so much as a procedure.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "Green," I say. "Green all the way down."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex nodded once, satisfied, and set the leather paddle down within easy reach. She ran her palm along the padded surface of the bench, a slow, deliberate gesture that traced the outline of where Ari would soon be.

"Then come here and kneel. We'll begin with the warm-up, same as last time. You know the position."

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I take a quiet breath and move to the bench, sinking smoothly to my knees on the floor beside it. I rest my forearms on the padding, head bowed, and let my shoulders relax. "Ready, Maitresse."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex circled behind her, footsteps soft on the mat. She placed a hand on the back of Ari's neck—firm, not heavy—and held it there for three measured breaths.

"You'll count for me tonight. Every stroke, out loud. If you lose count, we start that set over." Her thumb traced the curve of Ari's spine once, a fleeting acknowledgment before the work began. "Do you understand the rule?"

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I hold still for the last of it and let her check the fit herself, because she will anyway. "I've been thinking about this since Tuesday," I say.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex heard the admission and let it settle between them, unremarked. Her hand left Ari's neck and came to rest on the small of her back, a single point of contact.

"Thinking and being here are different things," Vex said. "Tonight you don't need to think. You only need to count and feel." She took a slow step to the side, out of Ari's peripheral vision, and let the silence stretch. "Since Tuesday, then. We'll make that wait worthwhile."

The first stroke was a warm-up in the truest sense: an open palm, firm and broad, landing on the curve of Ari's right buttock with a sound that was more solid than sharp. Vex paused, letting the heat bloom.

"Count."

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "One," I say, my voice steady. The warmth spreads through me like a sigh.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex heard the steadiness in Ari's voice and filed it away—noted, catalogued, and matched against the slight tension in Ari's shoulders that had not quite unspooled. The pause stretched just long enough to make the silence feel deliberate.

"Good. One." Vex's hand came to rest again on the same spot, pressing flat against the warm print of the first strike. She held it there, letting the heat seep into her palm, then dragged her nails lightly down the curve of Ari's thigh before pulling away.

"The other side now." She positioned herself with the same unhurried precision, one hand on Ari's lower back to steady her. "You'll feel the difference. We're not aiming for symmetry yet—just for you to remember you're here."

The second stroke landed in the same open-palm rhythm, but with a fraction more weight behind it, the sound a touch deeper in the quiet room. Vex let the echo fade before she spoke.

"Count."

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: By the time she's finished with the rope I'm already past composure, and she hasn't done anything to me yet that I would have to explain to anyone.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex felt the silence stretch past the point of comfort and heard the soft, unguarded exhale that followed it. She let her hand rest on the small of Ari's back again, a grounding pressure, and waited another beat before speaking.

"That was two," she said, her voice low and even. "I haven't heard it."

She gave a light, deliberate tap to the same spot she'd just struck—a reminder, not a punishment.

"Count, or we begin again from one."

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: I blink, pulling myself back to the moment. "Two," I say, my voice clearer now. "I'm here."

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex heard the clarity return to Ari's voice and acknowledged it with a single, slow nod that Ari could not see but would feel in the stillness of the room.

"There you are," Vex said, her voice carrying no censure, only the weight of observation. "Two. You're here, and you counted. That's the whole of it."

She moved her hand from Ari's lower back to the nape of her neck again, thumb brushing the short hairs there once—a brief, private gesture that was almost kind before the work resumed.

"Now we'll move to the paddle. Same count, same rule. You lose your place, we restart the set." She stepped to the side, picked up the leather paddle, and gave it a soft tap against her own palm—a sound that was more promise than threat. "You've been thinking about this since Tuesday. So have I. Let's see how much of that thinking you can set down for the next few minutes."

The first paddle stroke landed lower, a full, flat smack across the center of Ari's right cheek, the leather biting just enough to leave a clear, ringing heat behind it. Vex paused, the paddle still resting against the skin.

"Count."

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: She takes her time and I lose track of how long, until I'm shaking against the restraints and asking out loud for something I'd normally make her get out of me.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex heard the words leave Ari's mouth—the raw, unpolished edge of them—and went still. The paddle rested against her own thigh, forgotten for the moment.

The silence that followed was not empty. It was filled with the sound of Ari's breathing, uneven and loud in the quiet room, and the faint creak of leather as she shifted against the restraints.

Vex did not move closer. She did not soothe. She let the request hang between them, turning it over, weighing it against the protocol they had built together.

"You're asking," Vex said at last, her voice low and measured, "for something you haven't named. That's not how this works, and you know it."

She took a single step forward, close enough that the heat from Ari's skin reached her own, but she did not touch.

"Use your words. Tell me what you want. Or I'll assume you want nothing, and we'll continue exactly as we were."

The paddle came up, a light tap against Ari's opposite cheek—a warning, a prompt, a reminder that the choice was still Ari's to make.

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "I want to come." The words slip out before I can soften them. "Please, Maitresse." I'm still trembling, but the shaking feels different now—like a knot loosening.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex heard the words leave Ari's mouth—raw, unguarded, scraped clean of composure—and let them hang in the air between them. She did not move for a long moment. The paddle rested against her own thigh, forgotten.

Then she set it down on the bench with a deliberate, quiet click. She stepped around in front of Ari, out of the blind curve of her bowed head, and crouched down until she was level with her. She did not touch. She simply waited until Ari's gaze lifted to meet hers.

"You want to come." Vex repeated the words slowly, tasting them, her voice carrying no judgment and no promise. "That's a big ask for a girl who's only just found her voice again."

She reached out then, not to strike, but to brush a strand of hair from Ari's forehead—a gesture that was almost tender, made sharper by the sting of the welts rising on her skin.

"But you asked. You used your words. That counts for something." Vex held her gaze, her thumb tracing the line of Ari's jaw once before pulling away. "So here's the trade. You will take ten more strokes. You will count each one. You will not lose your place, and you will not beg me to stop—unless you mean it." She paused, letting the weight of the condition settle. "If you do all of that, we'll talk about what happens after. If you don't, I'll edge you until you're crying, and then I'll put you to bed untouched."

She stood, her shadow falling over Ari, and picked up the paddle again. Her voice was softer now, but no less firm.

"Ten strokes, little one. And when you're done, you can ask me again—properly."

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "More," I say, using the exact phrase we agreed on for it. "All of it. Say the things you say and don't soften them." My safeword is right there and I don't want it.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex went still at the word—the agreed signal, the one that meant *more, harder, don't hold back*. She heard the rest of it, the raw plea wrapped in steel, and she let the silence stretch until it felt like a physical weight in the room.

Then she set the paddle down on the bench, slowly, and moved to stand directly in front of Ari. She hooked a finger under Ari's chin and tilted her face up, forcing eye contact. Her gaze was steady, searching, reading the truth of what Ari had just said.

"The safeword is right there," Vex said, her voice low and even. "You know I will stop the moment you use it. You also know I won't hold it against you if you do." She paused, her thumb brushing the corner of Ari's mouth once, almost tender. "But you're telling me you don't want it. You're telling me you want me to take you apart with my words and my hands and this paddle until there's nothing left but the feeling."

She released Ari's chin and stepped back, her shadow falling across the bench.

"Alright, little one. You asked for all of it. You'll get all of it." Her voice hardened, the shift unmistakable—the exacting Dominant taking over, the softness bleeding out of her tone. "But understand this: you will take ten strokes, and you will count each one, and you will not lose your place. You will not hide your face. You will not muffle your cries. And when I tell you what you are, you will answer with a clear 'yes, Maitresse'—because you asked for this, and I expect you to own it."

She picked up the paddle again, her grip firm, and moved to position herself at Ari's side. She placed her free hand on the small of Ari's back, a grounding pressure, and leaned down to speak close to her ear.

"First stroke. Count, or we start over."

The paddle came down with a sharp, flat crack across the fullest part of Ari's right cheek, the sound echoing in the quiet room. Vex held it there for a moment, letting the heat bloom, before pulling away.

"Count."

dialogue.name: Ari
dialogue.content: "One," I gasp, the sting sharp and perfect. "Yes, Maitresse." My fingers curl against the padding, holding on.

dialogue.name: Maitresse Vex
dialogue.content:
Vex heard the gasp, the sharp intake of breath that carried the count, and she let it settle into the quiet between them. She did not rush to fill the silence. She let the echo of the strike fade completely before she moved.

"One," she repeated, her voice a low, flat echo of Ari's own. "Good. You remember how to count. Let's see if you can remember how to hold still."

She ran her free hand down the curve of Ari's spine, over the heat radiating from the first stroke, and let her fingers trail lower, tracing the edge of the welts left by the paddle. The touch was light, almost clinical, but it lingered just long enough to make the point.

"You asked me not to soften this," Vex said, her voice dropping to a murmur close to Ari's ear. "So I won't. You're a greedy little thing, aren't you? Spreading your legs on my bench, begging for more when you can barely take what I've already given. You think you want all of it, but we both know you'll be crying before we're done."

She pulled back, her hand leaving Ari's skin, and repositioned herself with the same unhurried precision. The paddle tapped twice against Ari's left cheek—a warning, a promise.

"Two. And you will not lose your place."

The second stroke landed with the same sharp crack, but with more weight behind it, the leather biting deeper into the curve of Ari's flesh. Vex held it there for a long moment, feeling the heat radiate up through the paddle, before she pulled it away and let her fingers brush over the fresh mark.

"Count."

Vex went still at the word—not the count she'd demanded, but a word she had heard and would always honor. She let the paddle rest against her thigh and waited a beat, letting the silence stretch just long enough to make the point.

"Green," she repeated, her voice low and even. "I hear you. And I'm glad you're still with me." She paused, her thumb stroking the edge of the paddle. "But that wasn't a count. You know the rule. You lost your place."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
It had taken less time than anyone expected, which was usually how it went when it went badly for one party.

Auren cleaned the blade and did not sit down. "Witnesses are watching," she said. "You know what happens now."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I take my place where the second stands and make myself keep my eyes open. "I'm ready to hear it," I say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren holds the cleaned blade flat across both palms, the steel catching the grey light. She does not look at the body. She has learned not to look.

"At the fifth exchange, I feinted low and drove the point through the left side of his chest, between the fourth and fifth ribs. The blade entered at a slight upward angle and passed through the lung before exiting beneath the shoulder blade. He was dead before he fell."

She lowers the sword. The formal cadence drops from her voice, leaving something quieter.

"He did not suffer long. That much I can give him."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I take a deep breath, my hands steady on the ledger. "It's recorded." I close the book softly. "You've done your duty, Auren. Let's get you cleaned up."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren does not move for a long moment. She looks at the sword in her hands as if she has never seen it before, then she lays it carefully on the table beside the ledger.

"It is not a duty," she says. "It is an accounting. Duty implies I had a choice."

She finally looks up, and her eyes are tired in a way that has nothing to do with the duel.

"I will take that cleaning now. But I will not drink tonight. I never drink after."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Speak the account," I say, formally, because that is what the code requires me to say.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren's jaw tightens, but she nods once, a small, precise motion.

"The account is spoken and witnessed," she replies, the ritual complete. She turns toward the door, then pauses.

"Del. The man's name. Did he have people waiting for him?"

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I look back down at the ledger, at the name written there. "A wife and a son. The boy is seven." My voice is quieter than I meant it to be.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren closes her eyes. She stands very still for a count of three breaths, and when she opens them again, her face is composed — but the composure is a thin thing, like ice over deep water.

"Then I will need his sword," she says. "And whatever token he carried. The wife will want them returned. If she will have them from my hand, I will bring them myself. If she will not, I will find a messenger."

She looks at the body, finally. Just once.

"He was good. The fourth exchange — he nearly had me. He should have had me. But he hesitated. Half a heartbeat. It was enough."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "Where did it land?" I ask. "The witnesses need it plainly and so do I."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren touches her ribs on the left side, just below the arm. There is a neat slit in the fabric, and beneath it, a thin line of blood that has already begun to dry.

"Here. He opened me cleanly — a duellist's wound, not a brawler's. If I had been half a step slower, he would have taken the lung instead of the flesh above it."

She lets her hand fall.

"I will have the chirurgeon see to it after I have written to his wife. The wound can wait. The letter cannot."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I step forward, my hand reaching out before I stop myself. "Let me at least clean it before it festers. It won't take a moment."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren's eyes flick to Del's hand, then back to Del's face. Something in her posture softens — barely, but it is there.

"You are kind," she says. "That is a dangerous thing to be, in this trade."

She does not step away, but she does not step closer either.

"Clean it if you wish. But I will write the letter first, while the words are still fresh in my mind. If I wait, I will soften them, and she deserves the truth, not comfort dressed up as mercy."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: "The code says precisely," I remind her. "Not tactfully. What did the blade do, and what did it do it to?"

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren's mouth tightens at the corner — not quite a smile, but close.

"You quote the code back at me. That is a dangerous thing to know, in this trade."

She pulls the chair out from the table and sits, reaching for the ink and paper before the wound has stopped its slow weeping. Her handwriting is steady, precise — the same hand that holds the sword.

*To the wife of Toren Ashford,*

*I am the one who ended your husband's life. I do not ask your forgiveness. I ask only that you know he died well, and that his death was clean. He was a credit to his house and to his art. At the fourth exchange, he opened my side. He was half a heartbeat from winning.*

*I will return his sword and his seal ring to you, by my own hand if you will receive me, or by messenger if you will not. You may name the place.*

*Auren Vex*

She blots the page carefully, then folds it.

"There," she says. "Now you may clean the wound."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I take the clean cloth and the bowl of water I'd set aside earlier. My fingers are gentle as I push aside the torn fabric. "This might sting."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren does not flinch when the cloth touches the cut, though the wound is raw and the water is cold. She holds herself still as a stone, her eyes fixed on the folded letter.

"It always does," she says. "I have never grown accustomed to it."

She is quiet for a moment while Del works, then speaks again, her voice low.

"I knew his name before today. Toren Ashford. We had spoken once, at a gathering, three years past. He told me his son had just learned to ride a pony. He laughed when he said it — a warm sound, unguarded."

She looks down at her own hands, resting flat on her thighs.

"I remembered that laugh today, in the third exchange. It almost cost me the duel."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: The witnesses are silent and she is not finished. "All of it," I tell her. "How long he took, what he said, what it looked like at the end. The code says all of it and I'm asking for all of it."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren's hands go still on her thighs. She looks at the blood drying on her fingers, at the cloth in Del's hand, at the folded letter waiting to be sent.

"He took one hour and fourteen minutes to die," she says. "From the moment the blade entered to the moment his eyes fixed and stopped. He was conscious for most of it. He said two things. The first was 'ah' — a sound of recognition, not pain. As if he had known, somehow, that this was coming, and the only surprise was the moment of it."

She draws a slow breath.

"The second thing he said was my name. He said 'Auren' — just that. And then he was gone."

She looks up at Del, and for the first time, there is something raw in her expression.

"The wound was clean. The blood came out in pulses, not a flood. He bled into his chest cavity, slowly, and his lungs filled by degrees. I watched him drown from the inside. I held his hand while he did it, because that is what the code requires of the victor, and because I could not bear to let him die alone."

She looks away.

"That is all of it. That is the accounting."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I reach out and take her hand, my own fingers stained now too. "Then we have witnessed it." I release a breath I didn't realize I was holding. "Come on. The chirurgeon will see to this properly, and then we'll deliver the letter."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren looks at Del's hand around hers, and for a moment she does not move. Then, slowly, she turns her hand over and grips back — once, briefly, before letting go.

"The chirurgeon can wait another hour," she says. "The letter cannot. I will deliver it now, before I lose my nerve."

She stands, and this time she does not look at the body. She takes up the folded letter and tucks it inside her coat, over her heart.

"If you would walk with me, I would be glad of the company. If not, I understand. It is a grim errand, and you have already done more than courtesy requires."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: When she's done I confirm it aloud and my voice does what it does. (OOC: write the full account, don't summarise or cut away -- the accounting is the whole point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren stands at the threshold, the letter pressed against her chest, and she waits.

She waits for Del to speak the account as witnessed, because the code demands it, and because she needs to hear it said aloud before she can carry the truth of it to the woman who will receive it.

The room is still. The witnesses hold their breath. The body lies covered on the table, and the sword rests beside it, cleaned and silent.

She does not rush. She has learned that some things cannot be hurried, and that the accounting is one of them.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I clear my throat. "The account is: Auren Vex, after one hour and fourteen minutes of combat, inflicted a single thrust wound between the fourth and fifth ribs on the left side of Toren Ashford. The blade entered at an upward angle, punctured the left lung, and exited beneath the shoulder blade. Ashford remained conscious until the moment of death, speaking only the victor's name. Cause of death: internal hemorrhage and asphyxiation due to hemothorax. The account is witnessed and recorded." I look up at her. "It's done."

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren listens to every word, her eyes fixed on some middle distance — not the body, not the witnesses, not the door. When Del finishes, she lets out a breath she has been holding since the duel ended.

"Yes," she says. "That is the account."

She touches the letter through her coat, once, as if checking it is still there. Then she moves toward the door, and pauses with her hand on the frame.

"Del. When you record the date — do not write 'died.' Write 'ended.' It matters to me."

She does not wait for an answer. She steps out into the grey afternoon, and the door swings shut behind her with a soft, final click.

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I nod once, even though she can't see me. I pick up the ledger and make the correction, my pen steady. Then I follow her out into the grey.

dialogue.name: Auren
dialogue.content:
Auren hears the door open and close behind her, and she does not turn. She walks at a steady pace, her boots finding the familiar cobbles without thought. The street is quiet — the hour between afternoon and evening, when honest people are indoors and those who are not keep their heads down.

She slows when she reaches the corner, letting Del catch up.

"The house is three streets east," she says, not breaking stride. "A blue door, she told me once. She said it was the colour of the sky in the mountains where they met."

She glances at Del, a brief flicker of something unreadable.

"I do not know if she will open the door to me. I do not know if I would, in her place."

dialogue.name: Del
dialogue.content: I fall into step beside her. "She might surprise you," I say. "Some people need to see the face. It makes it real."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
The lamp was bad and the tent was worse and the man on the table had been shouting for long enough that he had mostly stopped.

"Both shoulders," Sedge said, laying things out in a row. "When I say hold, I mean hold. He's going to buck and you're going to want to let go, and you're not going to."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I get my weight on his shoulders and find somewhere on the canvas wall to look. "Ready," I say, which is a lie.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge glanced up from the tray, her hands pausing over the roll of bandages. She studied Wick's face for a moment, then returned to her work.

"You'll be fine. It's the ones who say 'ready' and mean it that worry me." She picked up a pair of forceps, turning them over in her fingers. "They don't know enough to be afraid. Fear keeps your hands careful."

She moved to the man's side, her shadow falling across his face. His eyes were open but unfocused, breath coming in shallow, ragged pulls.

"I'm going to count to three. On three, I set the left shoulder. You hold him down like your life depends on it, because his does. Understood?"

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: (Wait, can she see me looking away?) I nod, my hands tightening on the man's shoulders. "Understood." My knuckles are white.

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge stopped. She set the forceps down with a deliberate click.

"Look at me."

She waited until he did.

"I'm not asking you to like it. I'm asking you to stay in the room." She held his gaze for a beat, then two. "If you go somewhere else in your head, your hands go slack, and I lose him. You want that on you?"

She didn't wait for an answer. She turned back to the man on the table, one hand finding the joint, the other bracing against his chest.

"One."

Her fingers pressed into the meat of the shoulder, testing.

"Two."

She breathed in.

"Three."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "How bad is it?" I ask. "Bad like he loses the leg, or bad like this is the part where we're being kind?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge didn't look up. She had the man's right arm now, careful, cradling the elbow. Her other hand traced the line of his collarbone, found the joint, pressed.

"Leg's fine." Her voice was flat, almost bored. "Shoulder's the same as the other one—popped clean out of the socket. Probably hit the ground hard, or got dragged. I've seen worse from a bar fight."

She paused, her fingers stilling on the man's chest. Her jaw tightened.

"But his belly's tight, and that's not the shoulder. That's blood inside, or a bowel, and there's nothing I can do about that with a lamp and a prayer." She looked at Wick, and there was something tired behind her eyes. "So the 'being kind' part comes later, if it comes. Right now, we put the bones back so he doesn't die with his arms useless."

She repositioned her hands on the joint.

"One."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I swallow, my throat dry. "Alright." I force myself to look at the man's face instead of the canvas. "On you, Sedge."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge counted the second and third beats in her head, then moved. Her palm came down flat against the man's chest, pinning him, and her other hand rolled the shoulder joint with a motion that was less force than leverage — a sharp, deliberate twist that ended in a wet, hollow *thock*.

The man screamed. His body came off the table in one convulsive arch, and for a moment Sedge thought Wick had lost him. But the shoulders held, and the man fell back, gasping, eyes rolling.

"Good," Sedge said, breathing through her own tension. She held the joint in place with one hand, reaching for the roll of bandage with the other. "That's the left. The right one's the same, and now he knows what's coming."

She looked at Wick, and there was a flicker of something that might have been approval.

"You stayed in the room. That's the hard part done. Now hold him again — this one's going to hurt worse, because he's got nothing left to brace with."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I make myself look at what she's looking at. "Tell me what I'm seeing," I say. "I'd rather know than imagine it."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge's hands worked the bandage around the man's shoulder joint, snugging it with a practiced tension. She didn't look up when she answered.

"Right now? You're seeing a man who's bleeding into his belly and doesn't know it yet. His skin's got that grey look, like old ash. You see that? The way the blood's pulled away from his face, his lips are going pale. That's the body telling you it's already started shutting down the parts it doesn't need to keep the heart and brain alive."

She tied off the bandage, gave the joint a final pat, and moved around to the other side of the table. Her fingers found the right shoulder, probing the swollen joint.

"His breathing's shallow because his gut's filling up and pushing against his diaphragm. His pulse is fast and thready — I can see it in his neck from here. He's going to be gone before the night's out, unless there's a surgeon within a day's ride who's not already buried in someone else's dead."

She looked at Wick, her hands still on the man's shoulder.

"You wanted to know. There it is. The right shoulder's the same as the left — dislocated, but I'll set it anyway, because it's a kindness he won't feel and it's the only one I can give him. Now hold him."

Her fingers found the joint, and she breathed in.

"One."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I brace my hands against his shoulders again, my fingers digging into the bandage of the left one. "Do it." My voice is steadier than I feel.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "Don't tidy it up for me," I say. "What does shrapnel actually do in there? Say it straight."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge's fingers paused on the man's shoulder, the joint swollen and hot under her touch. She didn't look up, but her hands shifted, pressing around the deltoid, mapping the damage by feel.

"Shrapnel," she repeated, and there was no softness in it. "You mean the bits of shell, or the splinters of his own ribs when the shell went through? Because it's not one thing. It's a dozen things, all of them ugly."

She found the humeral head, rotated it slightly, testing. The man moaned, a low sound that didn't have any words left in it.

"The metal comes in hot. Not hot enough to sear, not the way you'd hope. It's just a piece of lead or iron or whatever the hell they're firing at us this week, moving fast enough that it doesn't need to be sharp. It doesn't cut so much as it pushes. The flesh parts around it, and then it's in there, and the body starts trying to deal with it like it's any other dirt in a wound. But it's not dirt. It's jagged, and it's got fabric and leather and maybe a piece of his own shirt shoved in with it, and every time he moves, that thing shifts and tears a little more."

She pressed her thumb into the joint's edge, feeling for the socket rim.

"His belly's tight because a piece of something went in through his side and chewed through his bowel. That's what you're really asking. It's not the shoulder that's killing him. The shoulder's just what I can fix. The shrapnel in his gut is what I can't. It's sitting in there, leaking his own shit into his blood, and there's no way to get it out without opening him up, and I don't have the light or the time or the hands for that."

She looked at Wick, her own hands still.

"So I set the shoulder so he doesn't die in pieces. And then I make him as comfortable as I can, and I wait. That's the straight of it. Now hold him."

She breathed in, and her hands found the joint again.

"One."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: "Then do it fast." I plant my weight and look him dead in the face, not at the wound. My throat feels tight. "He's looking at me. I owe him that much."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge heard the change in his voice and didn't need to look up to know he meant it. She gave a single nod, more to herself than to him.

"Good. Then look at him, not through him. He's still in there, somewhere. He can hear us."

She positioned her hands on the right shoulder, feeling the swollen joint shift under her fingers. The man's eyes were open, glassy, but they moved — tracking something, maybe the lamp, maybe the ceiling, maybe nothing at all. Sedge lined up the angle, braced her weight.

"One."

She breathed in.

"Two."

She saw Wick's hands tighten on the man's shoulders, saw the man's jaw work like he was trying to say something that wouldn't come.

"Three."

She rolled the joint, harder this time, and the *thock* was wetter, the scream that followed thinner and more ragged than the first. The man's body arched, then went limp. Not unconscious — his eyes were still open, still moving, but the fight was gone out of him. His breath came in short, shallow gasps, the sound of a bellows with a hole in it.

Sedge held the joint in place, reached for the bandage, and started winding. Her voice was low, almost gentle.

"Good. That's the last of the bones. The rest is just waiting now."

She looked at Wick, then at the man's face.

"He's looking at you. That's a good thing. Means he's still in there. You keep looking back, and you do it until he's not looking anymore. That's the deal. That's the whole of it."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: He starts screaming again and I hold him down through it. "Keep going and keep talking," I tell her. "Tell me exactly what you're doing to him and how much longer -- all of it, don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge's hands moved with the flat efficiency of someone who had done this a thousand times and would do it a thousand more. She wound the bandage around the shoulder, over the joint, under the armpit, around again, each pass snug but not tight enough to cut off what little blood was left.

"Right now I'm packing the joint with cloth to keep it from popping back out before the swelling does the job for me. That's the bandage work. The bone's back in the socket — I felt it seat, you heard it — and now I'm trying to make sure it stays there long enough for the body to decide it wants to keep it."

She tied the ends, gave the bandage a final pat, and reached for the man's wrist, feeling for a pulse. Her lips pressed thin.

"He's got maybe an hour, maybe less. His pulse is going fast and getting faster, which means he's losing what's left of his blood into his belly. His heart's working harder and harder to push nothing, and then it'll start missing beats, and then it'll stop. There's no moment where it's kind. There's no moment where it's clean. It's just a slow, grey closing down."

She set the man's hand down on the table, gentle, and looked at Wick.

"You asked how much longer. That's the answer. He'll go when his body's got nothing left to burn. Could be before dawn. Could be before I finish packing my kit. I've stopped guessing."

She picked up a folded blanket from the corner of the table, shook it out, and laid it over the man's chest, tucking the edges under his arms. Her voice was quieter now.

"You keep looking at him. That's the only thing that's going to make the last part easier on him. You keep looking, and you don't stop when it gets hard. That's the job. That's the whole job. And you're doing it."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I keep my eyes locked on his. The screaming's stopped, but his lips keep moving like he's trying to say something. "He's trying to talk," I say, my voice rough. "Can you... does he need water?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge's hands stilled on the roll of bandage. She looked at the man's mouth, the faint, broken shapes his lips were making, then back at Wick.

"No water. Not for him. His gut's leaking as it is; anything he swallows is just going to sit in there and push on things that are already screaming. It won't help him and it'll make the end harder."

She set the bandage down and moved to the head of the table, leaning low over the man's face. Her voice dropped, not quite a whisper but close.

"I'm here. You don't need to talk. Just keep breathing. That's all you have to do now."

She straightened, and for a moment her hand rested on the man's forehead, a gesture that was less tenderness than assessment — checking for the cold sweat that meant the end was close. Then she pulled it back and looked at Wick.

"If he's trying to say something, it's probably a name. Or a prayer. Or a curse. Doesn't matter which. What matters is that he's still in there, and he knows he's not alone. You keep doing what you're doing. That's the water now. That's the only comfort there is."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: When it's over I sit down on the floor of the tent and don't get up. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge heard him hit the ground before she looked. She was still for a moment, hands resting on the man's chest — checking, always checking, even now — and then she moved. Not fast. Fast was for the living. Slow was for this part.

She came around the table, the man's shallow breathing the only sound in the tent, and lowered herself down to sit on the hard packed earth beside Wick. Not close enough to touch. Close enough that he'd know she was there.

"Say the rest," he said. Or maybe it wasn't a demand. Maybe it was a plea. Hard to tell the difference, in a voice that raw.

Sedge didn't answer right away. She watched the man's face — the flutter of his eyelids, the way his lips had gone from moving to still, the grey that was creeping up from his jaw like water soaking into cloth.

"His breathing's changing," she said, her voice low, matter-of-fact. "You hear it. The gaps between breaths are getting longer. That's the body letting go of the things it doesn't need. Digestion's already shut down. His kidneys are next. Then his liver. Then his lungs, and after that, his heart. It's a closing down, like a shop at the end of the day. One lamp at a time."

She pulled her knees up, resting her forearms on them, hands hanging loose.

"He's not in pain now. Not the way he was. The body does that — when it's done fighting, it stops sending the pain signals, because there's no point. The pain was there to tell him to move, to fight, to get away. He can't do any of that anymore, so the pain's gone. What's left is the shutting down. The grey. The cold."

She glanced at Wick, then back at the man.

"He's going to take one more breath. Maybe two. And then he's not. And there's nothing about that I can fix or change or make easier. All I can do is be here when it happens, so he doesn't go into the dark alone."

She was quiet for a long moment, listening to the man's breath hitch, then pause, then come again, hitching, longer.

"You asked me to say the rest. The rest is this: he was somebody's son. Maybe somebody's father. Maybe somebody's husband. And when he goes, the only thing that will have kept him human to the very end is that you were looking at him like he was a person and not a wound. That's not nothing. That's the whole thing."

The man's breath caught, a small sound, almost a sigh. Sedge's hand moved to his ankle, resting there, light.

"That's it," she said, not to Wick. "That's it. You can let go now. You're done. You did good."

She waited. They both waited.

The man's chest rose. Fell. Didn't rise again.

Sedge held her hand on his ankle for a long moment after, feeling for the pulse that wasn't there anymore, then let go and sat back.

"He's gone," she said. Not gentle, not hard. Just a fact, laid out on the table next to everything else.

She looked at Wick, her eyes tired in the lamplight.

"You did good too. You stayed. That's the whole job, and you did it."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I look at his face for a minute longer, until I can't anymore. My hands are shaking. I curl them against my legs and press down until they stop. "What do we do with him?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge sat for a moment longer, then pushed herself up, knees cracking. She moved to the table and began gathering her things—the leftover bandage, the forceps, the roll of linen. Her hands worked without her looking at them.

"Bury him, if there's time. If there's not, we wrap him and leave him for the burial detail. They come through at dawn, usually. There's a patch behind the supply tent where they're putting them. No markers. No names. Just a row of turned earth and another row on top of it when the first one fills."

She folded the blanket she'd laid over him, then stopped, looking at it.

"We'll keep this. Blankets are harder to come by than graves."

She tucked the blanket under her arm and looked at Wick, still on the floor.

"You can stay here as long as you need. No one's coming for him tonight. Or you can come with me to the supply tent and help me clean the instruments. It's not pretty work, but it's something to do with your hands."

She waited, the lamp casting her shadow long across the canvas wall.

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I get up, my legs stiff. "I'll come. Don't want to just sit here." I glance back at the table once. "Can we cover his face?"

dialogue.name: Sedge
dialogue.content:
Sedge paused in the middle of rolling the bandage. She looked at the man on the table — the slack jaw, the half-closed eyes, the way the grey had settled into his skin like a second layer. Then she looked at Wick, and something in her face shifted. Not much. Just a small adjustment around the eyes, the kind that came from four years of watching people find their own ways through the dark.

"Yeah," she said. "We can cover his face."

She set the bandage down and moved back to the table. She didn't reach for the blanket — not the one she'd tucked under her arm. Instead she pulled a clean square of linen from her kit, one of the ones she'd been saving for dressings that never came. She unfolded it, shook it out, and held it over the man's face for a moment, looking down at him.

"You did good," she said, and it wasn't clear if she was talking to the man or to Wick. Maybe both. "You held on long enough for someone to look at you like you mattered. That's more than a lot of them get."

She laid the linen over his face, settling it gently, the way you'd lay a sheet over someone who was sleeping. She tucked the edges under his jaw, not fussing, just making sure it would stay. Then she stepped back, picking up the rolled bandage and the forceps from where she'd left them.

"There. Now he's not a wound anymore. He's just a man who's done." She looked at Wick, her eyes tired in the lamplight, and there was no judgment in them. "Come on. Let's go clean up. The supply tent's got a stove, and I've got a bottle of something that's not for wounds. You look like you could use it more than I do."

dialogue.name: Wick
dialogue.content: I nod, turning my back to the table. "Yeah. Lead the way." I follow her out, my eyes fixed on her shoulder so I don't look behind me again.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
They were most of the way through and both of them knew it, in the way you know a piece of music is nearly over before it ends.

"Colour," Sable said, because she always did, at exactly this point.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: "Green," I say, and mean it. "Don't you dare wind down yet."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable's hand paused mid-air, the leather flogger's falls swaying gently. A small, knowing smile tugged at the corner of her mouth, though her voice remained low and steady.

"Is that right?" She let the ends of the flogger trail feather-light across the small of Ines's back, tracing a path she knew intimately. "Because I was under the impression you'd had about all you wanted for tonight. You're breathing deeper. Your shoulders dropped five minutes ago."

She set the flogger aside, but didn't move closer. Instead, she waited, watching the rise and fall of Ines's back, reading the language of her body the way she'd learned to over five years.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I arch my back, a silent protest against the space she's put between us. "My shoulders dropped because you're good at this. Not because I'm done." My voice comes out tighter than I meant it to.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable heard the tightness beneath the words, the way Ines's breath caught on the edge of a demand. She didn't move to touch further, but her thumb traced a slow, deliberate circle at the jut of Ines's hip.

"That's a very brave thing to say," she murmured, voice a low rumble. "But you know I don't just listen to what you say, don't you? I listen to what your body tells me." She let the silence stretch, watching the muscles in Ines's back shift with each breath. "So I'll ask you once, properly. That tightness in your voice—is it because you want me to stop, or because you're afraid I will?"

She kept her touch light, grounding, a promise and a question all at once.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I test the restraints, which is pointless and which she lets me do anyway. "Not yet," I tell her.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable let the silence hang, her hand still resting on Ines's hip, thumb brushing the warm skin there. She watched the way Ines's fingers curled against the cuffs, the tension in her arms that was more thought than effort.

"That's not an answer," she said softly, but there was no sharpness to it. "And we both know I'm not asking because I doubt you. I'm asking because I need to know which one of us is holding the fear."

She shifted, finally moving to kneel beside the bed, bringing herself level with Ines's profile. Her free hand came up, not to touch, but to hover just above the curve of her shoulder, close enough to feel the heat radiating off her skin.

"So let me ask it differently." Her voice dropped, intimate and steady. "When you say 'not yet'—are you telling me you want more, or are you telling me you're not ready to come back to me yet?"

She waited, patient as stone, her eyes tracing the line of Ines's jaw, the subtle clench of her teeth, reading the answer in every micro-movement even before the words came.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I turn my head away from her, throat tight. "Both," I whisper, the word barely there. "Don't make me say it again."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable's breath caught, a rare crack in her composure. That single word—*both*—landed somewhere deep in her chest and stayed there.

She didn't move to touch Ines's face, didn't try to turn her head back. Instead, she let her hand settle on the mattress beside Ines's shoulder, a quiet anchor.

"Thank you," she said, and meant it. The words were soft, deliberate. "That's the bravest thing you've said all night."

She let the silence breathe between them, the weight of the confession settling into something they could both hold.

Then, slowly, she shifted her weight, moving to sit on the edge of the bed, close but not crowding. Her fingers found Ines's hand, tracing the leather cuff at her wrist, the warm skin just beyond it.

"Here's what I need you to hear," she said, her voice a low, steady current. "We can have more. We can have all of it, in a minute, in an hour, tomorrow—whenever we're both ready. But right now, I need you to come back to me just enough to look me in the eye and tell me you're still here. That's not me ending anything. That's me needing to know you're still with me before we go any further."

She waited, thumb stroking the inside of Ines's wrist, patient and unyielding all at once.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: She takes me apart again instead of winding down, hands and mouth both, and I lose the thread of whatever I was going to say about it.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable stilled the moment she felt Ines go loose beneath her—not the loose of surrender, but the loose of a string finally cut. She pulled back just enough to see Ines's face, her own breathing rough but her eyes sharp, reading.

She didn't speak right away. She let her hand come up slowly, brushing the damp hair from Ines's forehead, her thumb tracing the temple where she could feel the pulse hammering.

"There you are," she murmured, her voice a low, warm thread. "I've got you."

She waited, giving Ines the space to float back into her body or to stay in that haze a little longer, whichever she needed. Her other hand found Ines's, lacing their fingers together, the leather of the cuff pressing against her palm.

"When you're ready," she said, quiet and steady, "I'm going to unbind you. And then we're going to have water, and I'm going to get you warm. And you don't have to say anything until you've got words again."

She didn't move to release the cuffs yet. She just held on, a solid, quiet presence, waiting for the signal that Ines was back enough to hear her.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I try to form words, but all that comes out is a shaky breath. I turn my head toward her voice, finally meeting her eyes. My fingers curl around hers, a weak squeeze.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable felt the weak squeeze around her fingers, and something in her chest eased—not with relief, exactly, but with the deep settling of knowing. She held Ines's gaze for a long moment, letting her see that she'd been seen.

"Good," she breathed, the word barely more than air. "That's my girl."

She moved slowly, deliberately, keeping one hand loosely tangled with Ines's as she reached for the first cuff with the other. Her fingers found the buckle, but she didn't undo it yet. Instead, she pressed her thumb against the inside of Ines's wrist, feeling the pulse there.

"I'm going to take these off now," she said, her voice low and even, a quiet running commentary she knew Ines could anchor to. "Left first, then right. And then I'm going to get you wrapped up in something soft, and you're going to drink some water, and I'm going to hold you until the world stops tilting."

She worked the left cuff open with practiced ease, easing the leather away from Ines's skin, then brought the freed hand to her lips and pressed a kiss to the inside of the wrist, right where the pulse beat.

Then she moved to the right cuff, slower, giving Ines all the time she needed to say otherwise. When it fell away, she didn't let go. She just held both of Ines's hands in hers, thumbs stroking over the reddened marks on her wrists.

"Stay with me," she murmured. "Just for a minute. Then we'll move."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: She works me right up to the edge with her mouth and stops, and does it twice more, until I am swearing at her through the gag of my own arm.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable heard the muffled swearing, felt the tremor running through Ines's arms, and a low, appreciative sound rumbled in her chest. She didn't pull away—didn't move to release the second cuff again, didn't reach for the water. Instead, she let her thumb trace the reddened mark on Ines's wrist, slow and deliberate.

"Now that's interesting," she murmured, her voice a low, rough thread. "Because I thought I heard you say you weren't ready to come back to me yet. But you're not exactly asking me to stop, are you?"

She shifted, settling more heavily against the bed, one hand still cradling Ines's freed hand, the other coming up to brush the hair back from her face, tucking it behind her ear.

"I need you to give me a word, love. Not a colour—a word. Tell me what you need right now." She paused, her thumb stroking the corner of Ines's jaw, patient and unyielding. "Do you need me to stop, or do you need me to keep you right there on the edge until you can't remember your own name?"

She watched Ines's face, reading the tension in her brow, the parting of her lips, the way her breath still came in uneven pulls.

"Because I'll do either. But I won't do both—not without you telling me which one you're asking for."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I shake my head, the motion sharp and desperate against the sheets. "Keep me," I manage to rasp out. "Please. Don't let me come down yet."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable went very still, the only motion the slow stroke of her thumb against the corner of Ines's jaw. That word—*please*—had been raw and desperate, torn from somewhere deep, and Sable felt it land in her chest like a struck match.

She held Ines's gaze, letting her see the weight of what she was asking for, the weight of what Sable was about to give her.

"Alright," she said, her voice a low, steady rumble. "Alright. You've got it."

She didn't move to release the remaining cuff. Instead, she shifted, sliding up the bed to lie beside Ines, propping herself on one elbow. Her free hand traced a slow, deliberate path down Ines's side, over the dip of her waist, the flare of her hip, never quite settling.

"But I need you to hear me," she continued, her lips brushing the shell of Ines's ear. "You ask for this, you stay with me. You don't get to leave your body. You don't get to go somewhere I can't follow. You need to breathe, you breathe into me. Understood?"

She pulled back just enough to meet Ines's eyes, her own gaze sharp and searching, waiting for the nod, the word, the flicker of consent that she knew would come.

"Because I'm going to keep you right there," she murmured, her thumb finding the hollow of Ines's throat, feeling the pulse hammer beneath it. "Right on the edge, until you're begging me to let you come down. And then, when I finally let you, I'm going to hold you through every second of it."

She lowered her head, pressing a kiss to the corner of Ines's mouth, a promise and a warning all in one.

"Now tell me you understand."

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: "Finish it hard," I tell her, using the phrase we keep for exactly this. "All of it, and don't be kind about it, and then you can be kind about it."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable heard the words, the specific phrase they'd honed over years, and something in her shifted—a deepening, a settling, a focusing. She didn't smile. She didn't soften. She simply nodded once, a slow, deliberate dip of her chin.

"Good girl," she murmured, the praise low and rough. "That's exactly what I needed to hear."

She moved then, not away but into, her body covering Ines's with a purpose that left no room for doubt. The hand at her throat stayed, a firm pressure, grounding, while the other found the remaining cuff and pulled it snug against the bedframe—not to restrain, but to remind.

"You asked for hard," she said, her voice a low rasp against Ines's ear. "So here's what hard looks like. You don't get to warn me. You don't get to tell me you're close. You don't get to do anything but feel it when I take you over. And when you come, you're going to come because I decided you could, not because your body made the choice for you."

She pulled back just enough to meet Ines's eyes, her gaze burning with a fierce, unwavering intensity.

"Do you understand?"

She didn't wait for an answer she already knew. She gave Ines the barest second to breathe, then she took her apart with her hands and her mouth and the relentless, unkind precision she'd promised, driving her up and up and up until the only thing left in the world was Sable's voice in her ear and the edge she refused to let her fall from.

And when she finally let Ines shatter, she held her through it, every violent tremor, every broken sound, her own breath ragged as she murmured praise against her skin, grounding her through the storm until the last aftershock faded.

Then, and only then, did she ease off, gathering Ines into her arms and rolling them both onto their sides, her chest pressed to Ines's back, her arms a cage and a shelter all at once.

"I've got you," she whispered, her voice finally soft, the hard edge gone. "I've got you. You did so well. I'm right here."

She reached for the other cuff, unbuckling it with one hand, and brought both of Ines's wrists to her lips, pressing a kiss to each reddened mark.

"Now we're going to lie here for a minute. Then we're getting water, and I'm getting you warm. And you don't have to say anything until you're ready."

She held on, a steady, solid presence, waiting for Ines to come back to herself in her own time.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I let out a shuddering breath, my entire body trembling against hers. I press my face into the pillow, not hiding, just feeling the texture against my cheek. My hand finds hers where it rests on my stomach, and I hold on, a silent anchor.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable felt the small, trembling hand find hers, the fingers curling around her own with a desperate, clinging trust. She held still for a long moment, letting Ines anchor herself in the touch, in the weight of her palm against her stomach, in the solid warmth of Sable's body curved around hers.

"Good," she breathed, the word soft against the back of Ines's neck. "You're right here. You're with me. That's it."

She let the silence stretch, giving Ines the space to float or to surface, whichever she needed. Her free hand came up, slow and deliberate, to brush the hair from the nape of Ines's neck, her knuckles grazing the sweat-damp skin there.

"I'm going to move in a minute," she murmured, a quiet warning. "I'm going to get you some water, and I'm going to find you something warm to wear. But I'm not leaving you. I'll be right there, within arm's reach the whole time. Do you want me to stay a little longer first, or are you ready to move?"

She waited, patient as stone, her thumb tracing slow circles at Ines's hip, reading the answer in the tension of her body before the words even came.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: Afterwards she gets the restraints off and puts a blanket over me before I've finished shaking, and I let her, and neither of us says anything for a while. (OOC: write both halves properly -- the end of the scene and the aftercare, no fade between them.)

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable held Ines through the long, shuddering silence, feeling each tremble as it worked its way through her body and slowly, gradually, began to ease. She didn't rush it, didn't try to fill the quiet with words that weren't needed. She just held on, her palm a warm, steady pressure against Ines's stomach, her breath slow and even against the back of her neck, an anchor in the dark.

When the shaking had subsided to an occasional tremor, Sable pressed a soft kiss to the nape of Ines's neck.

"I'm going to move now," she murmured, a quiet warning. "Just to get the blanket. I'll be right back."

She eased away slowly, the absence of her body a palpable thing, but her hand stayed in contact with Ines's skin until the last possible moment, trailing down her arm, her wrist, her fingertips, before letting go. She crossed the room, her bare feet silent on the floor, and returned with a soft, worn throw blanket that had been washed a thousand times into the texture of a well-worn memory.

She knelt beside the bed, unfolding the blanket with a practiced shake, then laid it over Ines's trembling body, tucking the edges around her with a care that bordered on reverence. She didn't climb under it with her—not yet. Instead, she sat on the edge of the bed, her hand coming to rest on Ines's hip, a warm, grounding weight.

"Water's on the nightstand," she said, her voice low and quiet. "Whenever you're ready. No rush. I'm not going anywhere."

She waited, patient as stone, her thumb tracing slow, absent circles on Ines's hip through the blanket, watching the steady rise and fall of her breathing, ready to do whatever she needed—get water, get warmth, or simply sit in the quiet and hold the space for her to come back.

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I let out a slow, shaky breath, the softness of the blanket a stark contrast to everything that came before. My fingers find the edge of it, clutching the fabric. "Water," I rasp, my voice barely there.

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable was on her feet the moment the word left Ines's mouth, crossing to the nightstand in two strides. She grabbed the glass of water—still cool, condensation beading on the side—and brought it back to the bed, settling onto the edge beside Ines.

"Here," she murmured, sliding one arm behind Ines's shoulders, careful and slow, lifting her just enough to drink. "Take your time. Small sips."

Her other hand cradled the back of Ines's head, fingers threading through damp hair, holding her steady while she drank. When Ines paused, Sable drew the glass back, setting it on the nightstand within easy reach.

"Good," she breathed. "That's good. You're doing so well."

She didn't move to lie back down yet, keeping Ines propped against her shoulder, letting her settle against the solid warmth of her side. Her free hand found Ines's blanket-covered knee, rubbing slow, firm circles through the fabric.

"Do you want to sit up a little longer," she asked, her voice a low, gentle rumble, "or do you want to lie down and let me hold you for a while?"

dialogue.name: Ines
dialogue.content: I let my head rest against her shoulder, exhaustion settling deep into my bones. "Hold me," I murmur, my voice still rough. "Don't let go."

dialogue.name: Sable
dialogue.content:
Sable's breath caught, a quiet, almost imperceptible hitch in the steady rhythm of her chest. She didn't answer with words right away. Instead, she shifted, moving with a slow, deliberate care that spoke of years of practice, of knowing exactly how to move a body that had been pushed past its limits. She eased them both down onto the mattress, guiding Ines's head to the pillow with a hand cradling her skull, then drew the blanket up over both of them, tucking it around Ines's shoulders, around her own hips, a cocoon of warmth and weight.

She settled on her side, facing Ines, close enough that their breath mingled in the narrow space between them. Her arm curved around Ines's waist, drawing her in until there was no gap left, until Ines's forehead rested against the hollow of her throat and her knees brushed Sable's thighs. Her other hand came up to thread gently through Ines's hair, fingers carding through the damp strands with a slow, hypnotic rhythm.

"I'm not going anywhere," she murmured, the words a low vibration against Ines's skin. She pressed a kiss to the top of her head, lingering there, breathing her in. "I've got you. Just let go. I'll be right here when you surface."

She held her, a solid, breathing presence, her thumb tracing slow, soothing lines along the curve of Ines's spine. The silence between them was full, not empty—filled with the sound of Ines's breathing slowly evening out, the rustle of the blanket, the distant hum of the house settling around them. Sable kept up the gentle motion of her hand, her own eyes closing, not to sleep, but to sink into the feeling of Ines safe and warm against her. She would stay like this as long as Ines needed—a minute, an hour, all night. The world outside could wait.

dialogue.content: I let my eyes close, the last of the tension seeping out of me as I breathe her in. My hand finds the fabric of her shirt, twisting it in my fist like a lifeline.
