dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
The cellar had four feet of standing water in it and something at the far end that had stopped moving about a minute ago.

Halloway held the lamp up and did not go closer yet. "Right," she said. "Before we touch it. What do you see?"

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I make myself look properly instead of at the water. "I don't know yet," I say. "Something wrong with the shape of it."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content: Halloway grunted, shifting her weight so the lamp cast a longer angle across the water. "The head's too far back for a human neck. And the arms—if those are arms—are jointed wrong. Bent like a dog's hind leg but attached at the shoulder." She let that sit a moment. "Could be a corpse that's been in the water long enough to bloat and twist. Could be something that never walked upright to begin with."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I swallow hard, my throat tight. "The fingers... if they're fingers, there's too many of them." I point, my hand shaking a little. "See how they're splayed out? Like it was trying to climb the wall."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway studied the hand for a long moment, then nodded slowly. "That's not bloat-swelling. That's structural. The joints are in the wrong places." She lowered the lamp a fraction, casting the thing in deeper shadow. "Good eye. What else?"

She waited, letting the silence press. The water stank of old iron and wet stone, and somewhere above them a floorboard creaked.

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "Was that a person?" I ask. "Recently, I mean. Is that what I'm looking at?"

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway exhaled through her nose, a sound that might have been a laugh in a warmer room. "No. That's not a person any more, if it ever was." She tilted the lamp again, letting the light crawl over the thing's silhouette. "People don't grow extra finger joints in the time it takes to drown. And they don't—" she paused, "—they don't have that many teeth in a mouth that small."

She looked at Pike sidelong. "Whatever it is, it's been dead a while. Recently killed, maybe. But not recently *human*."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I nod, but my stomach is still twisting. "There's... something on the wall behind it. Scratches, maybe? Like it was trying to get away from something else."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway stepped sideways through the water, slow and deliberate, to get a better angle. The lamp threw her shadow huge and wavering across the stone. She studied the marks in silence.

"Not trying to get away," she said finally. "Trying to get *out*. These are too deep for warning scratches. It wore the stone down trying to dig through." She traced one of the grooves with her gaze. "Which means it wasn't running *from* something. It was trapped in here. And something put it here."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I wade closer and hold the lamp where she can work. "Tell me what happened to it," I say. "Plainly."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway crouched, the water lapping at her belt, and ran her free hand along the nearest groove. She didn't flinch at the cold or the slime.

"It was alive when it went in the wall. Those scratches are frantic—no pattern, no rhythm. Just panic." She straightened, wiped her hand on her thigh. "As for what killed it—" She pointed with the lamp. "See the chest? Caved in. Not from a blow. Something crushed it from the inside out. Ribs pushed outward, not broken inward. Sternum's gone."

She paused, letting that sink in.

"Whatever it was, it didn't die from the water or starvation. It died because something inside it decided to leave." She looked at Pike, flat and steady. "And whatever came out is probably still down here with us."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I take a shaky breath. "What do we do?" I keep my voice low, my eyes scanning the dark water around us. "If it's still here, it's quiet."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway didn't answer right away. She let the lamp hang low, her eyes moving slowly across the water's surface, then up the walls, then to the ceiling beams where the dark collected thick as tar.

"Then we stop assuming it's in a hurry," she said, quiet enough that the words didn't carry. "Whatever came out of that thing, it's had time to learn the layout. It knows we're here. It's not moving because it doesn't need to." She lifted the lamp a few inches, just enough to catch the nearest wall. "Could be watching us right now. Could be waiting for us to split up or turn our backs."

She looked back at Pike, and there was something almost like approval in the flat line of her mouth.

"So here's what we do. We back out the way we came. Slow. No sudden turns. We don't give it the satisfaction of running." She jerked her head toward the stairs. "And when we're back in the house, we burn the whole place down around this cellar. If it wants to hunt, it can hunt somewhere the rules don't favor it."

She took a half-step back, keeping her body between Pike and the dark water. "You take the lead. I'll keep the lamp on you. And if you hear me stop breathing, you don't turn around. You run."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: "I need the detail," I say. "Tell me exactly what it did to him -- what is under the skin now, what it took, how far it got. If I meet another one I need to know."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: *Halloway's gaze sharpens.* "It didn't just take organs. It hollowed him. Left the skin and bones like a sack. Whatever crawled out, it's wearing what it needs now." She starts backing toward the stairs. "Move, Pike. Lesson's over."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway's boots made soft, sucking sounds in the mud as she backed toward the stairs, the lamp still held low but ready. She didn't look away from the dark water, didn't give it the courtesy of a turned back.

"Lesson's not over yet," she said, her voice barely above a murmur. "It's just moved to the part where we don't get dead because we were too curious to leave."

She stopped at the bottom step, one foot on the worn stone, and finally risked a glance at Pike. Her face was hard, but there was a flicker of something beneath it—not fear. Caution, maybe. Or the kind of respect you only get from surviving long enough to know when to walk away.

"When we get to the top, you go straight out the front door. Don't stop for anything. Don't look back. I'll be right behind you, but if I'm not—" She let that hang, then gave a grim smile. "Well. You'll hear the screaming."

She waited, listening to the cellar's silence, to the water lapping gently against the walls. Then she nodded once, sharp, and started up the stairs backward, the lamp casting her shadow huge and jagged ahead of them.

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: She starts cutting and I hold the lamp steady and don't look away. "Keep describing it," I tell her. "Everything -- what's underneath, what it smells like, how far it got. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway knelt in the water, the blade of her knife already finding the seam where the thing's sternum should have been. She worked it in with a wet, grinding sound, and did not blink.

"Underneath," she said, her voice low and even, "there's no muscle to speak of. What's left of it is stringy, like it was chewed out from the inside. The ribs aren't broken—they're *spread*. Something pushed through them from within and didn't bother to close the door on the way out."

She pulled the cut wider, the lamp shaking just slightly in Pike's hand, and she paused to look up at them.

"Smell is the first thing you'll notice. It's not rot—not the kind you'd expect from something dead in water. It's sour. Metallic. Like old copper coins left to soak in vinegar. That's the blood, but it's not human blood anymore. It's thin, watery, and it smells like it's been cooking inside that thing for a long, long time."

She reached in with two fingers, and there was a soft, wet squelch as she pulled something free. She held it up to the lamp without a flicker of disgust.

"This is what's left of its heart. Except it's not a heart. Not shaped right. Too many chambers, and it's fused to the spine—grown into it, like it was never meant to come out. And it's *cold*. Not cold from the water. Cold like something that was never alive in the way we are."

She dropped it back into the chest cavity with a splash, then wiped her hand on her trousers, leaving a dark smear.

"How far it got?" She let out a breath, half a laugh, half a sigh. "All the way. It didn't just take the organs it needed to live. It took everything that made him *him*. The memories, the fear, the way he walked, the way he talked. It hollowed him out and wore him like a coat until it was done with him. Then it shed him here, in the dark, where no one would find him until the water brought him back."

She looked up at Pike, and for a moment there was something almost like pity in her eyes.

"Whatever you're planning to cut next, cut shallow. It's got a lot of surprises left in it, and I'd rather not be the one to find out what they are the hard way."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I take the knife from her hand, my own steady for the first time. "Show me where it started," I say, and start cutting along the thing's arm, following the strange bend of the bone.

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway watched Pike's hand work the blade, and a long, slow breath escaped her—not tension, exactly. Something closer to grim approval.

"Elbow's the wrong way for a start," she said, voice low. "But you picked the right joint. Whoever made that arm bent it at a shoulder that shouldn't have been there. You'll find the seam where it connects—it'll look like gristle, but it's not. It'll be pale, almost white, and it'll resist the blade no matter how sharp you are. That's not a tendon. That's the thing's way of keeping its coat on."

She shifted, the water rippling around her knees, and her eyes flicked to the dark water beyond Pike's shoulder before returning to the work.

"Once you cut through that, you'll see the inside of the limb is hollow. Not eaten out—*lined*. Like a sheath. Whatever it wore, it wore it from the inside out. You'll find the base of the skull is the real lock. That's where it got in. That's where it left."

She paused, letting Pike work in the silence for a moment.

"Go careful around the wrist. That's where it kept its hands. If you see something that looks like a knot of bone, don't cut it. It's got a habit of waking up when you do."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I sit on the cellar steps afterwards with the lamp in my hands. "Finish it," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full.)

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway took the knife back without a word, turning it over in her fingers once as if testing its balance. She gave Pike a long look—not a rebuke, just an assessment—then turned back to the thing in the water and set to work.

She started at the shoulder Pike had exposed, sliding the blade along the pale seam of gristle. It resisted, just as she'd said, the edge skidding slightly before finding the give. She pressed harder, and the material parted with a wet, reluctant sound, like tearing thick leather. She peeled the arm back from the torso, revealing the hollow interior—a smooth, glistening lining that caught the lamplight like wet silk.

"The sheath goes all the way down," she said, her voice low and even, narrating as she worked. "It's not attached to the skin. It's grown into it, like a second layer. You can see the texture—see how it's ridged? Those are the tracks it used to move inside. Like fingers inside a glove, except the glove was the whole body."

She reached into the hollow arm, her fingers disappearing up to the second knuckle. She felt around, her brow furrowed in concentration, then made a small sound of discovery.

"There. The knot of bone. It's not at the wrist—it's higher, in the forearm. See it?" She angled the arm so Pike could see, the lamp casting shadows into the open flesh. "That's where it kept its hands. It pulled them back up inside itself when it was done with them. That's why the fingers were splayed—it was still wearing them when it died."

She worked the knot free with the tip of the knife, and it came loose with a soft pop. She held it up—a small, dense cluster of bone, shaped like a closed fist. It was smooth, almost polished, and it glistened wetly in the lamplight.

"Not bone," she said. "Not exactly. Feels more like gristle that's been calcified. Hard as rock, though. You could take an edge to it and not leave a mark."

She set it aside on the stone floor, where it lay in the lamplight like a grotesque pearl.

"Now the head," she said, and turned to the thing's neck.

She worked the blade around the base of the skull, feeling for the seam where the thing had entered. She found it—a hairline crack that ran all the way around, just above the first vertebra. She slipped the knife in and twisted, and the skull came away in her other hand like a lid.

She held it up, letting the lamp shine inside. The interior was smooth, polished, the same glistening lining as the arm. There was no brain. Instead, a thick, milky cord ran down the center of the spine, disappearing into the neck.

"There it is," she said quietly. "That's the root. It grew a taproot, right down the spinal column, into the pelvis. It wasn't just wearing the body—it was *rooted* in it. That's how it learned to walk so well. That's how it knew how to talk. It wasn't mimicking. It was reading the memories straight off the nervous system."

She reached in with two fingers and touched the cord. It was cold, and it pulsed faintly—a slow, rhythmic throb that had nothing to do with the dead thing's heart.

"It's still alive," she said. "The root, I mean. The rest of it is dead as a doornail, but this—this is still waiting. Still thinking, maybe. It's the last piece of whatever crawled out of here."

She looked up at Pike, her face unreadable in the lamplight.

"You want me to finish it. Cut the cord, and whatever's left of it dies for good. Or we leave it, and we burn the place down around it, and hope the fire reaches deep enough."

She waited, the knife hovering over the cord, the water lapping gently against her knees.

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I reach out and touch the cord with the back of my hand. The cold of it seeps into my knuckles. "Cut it," I say. "I want to hear it die."

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway held Pike's gaze for a moment, then gave a single, slow nod. No smile, no satisfaction—just the acknowledgment of a job done right.

"Good," she said. "Then you'd better hold the lamp steady."

She shifted her grip on the knife, turning the blade so the edge caught the lamplight. The cord lay exposed, pale and pulsing, that faint rhythmic throb like a second heartbeat in the hollow of the dead thing's spine. She pressed the flat of the blade against it first, testing the resistance. It gave slightly, like tough gristle, and the pulsing quickened.

"Here we go," she murmured, and cut.

The cord parted with a sound like a wet mouth closing—a soft, sucking *pop* that echoed off the cellar walls. For a moment, nothing happened. The pulsing stopped, then started again, faster, desperate, as if the root were trying to find another way. The glistening lining of the arm rippled, and the hollow chest cavity gave a wet, convulsive shudder.

Then the cord began to wither.

It didn't rot or decay—it *shrank*, curling in on itself like a burning photograph, blackening at the edges and flaking away into a fine, dry dust. The root's frantic pulsing slowed, stuttered, and stopped. The body beneath the water went still. The ripple in the arm ceased. The thing that had worn this skin for so long was gone.

The silence that followed was complete. No water lapping. No creaking floorboards. Even the air seemed to hold its breath.

Halloway straightened slowly, the knife still in her hand, and looked down at the empty husk in the water. Then she looked at Pike, and there was something in her eyes that might have been the ghost of respect.

"That's the sound it makes," she said quietly. "When it dies for good."

She wiped the blade on her thigh—a slow, deliberate motion—and sheathed it. Then she held out her hand, palm up, waiting.

"Come on. We've got a house to burn."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I take her hand and let her pull me up. My fingers are still cold from the cord. "What do we use to start it?" I ask, my voice quiet in the sudden quiet.

dialogue.name: Halloway
dialogue.content:
Halloway's mouth twitched—the closest thing to a smile she'd offered all night.

"Kerosene," she said, "and a match. But if you're asking whether I came prepared for this, the answer is I've been ready to burn this house down since we set foot in it." She pulled a small, oil-stained tin from her coat pocket and held it up. "Two flasks of lamp oil, a rag, and a length of fuse. I've been carrying it since we walked in the front door."

She tucked the tin back into her coat and started toward the stairs, boots sloshing through the dark water without hesitation.

"The trick with cellars is you want the fire to start low and burn hot. Get the flames under the floorboards, and the whole house goes up like a candle. We'll soak the stairs, set the fuse, and be out the front door before the smoke even thinks about finding us."

She paused at the bottom step, looking back over her shoulder. Her face was half in shadow, the lamp catching only the hard line of her jaw.

"Unless you've got a better idea. But I'd rather not give that thing the chance to learn how to crawl back into something else."

dialogue.name: Pike
dialogue.content: I shake my head. "No, that's good. Just... let's be quick about it." I follow her up the stairs, trying not to look back at the hollow thing in the water.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
The ambush had gone the way ambushes go when they work: fast, and then over, and then very quiet. Wrack was crouched by the ditch cleaning her knife on a dead man's cloak, which was the only clean cloth within reach.

"Six," she said, without looking up. "Count again if you want, but it's six." She tested the edge against her thumb. "One of them's still making noise, off past the cart. You'll want to decide what you're doing about that before it gets dark."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I wipe my face with the back of my wrist and it comes away wet. Not mine, I think. "I heard him," I say. I don't move toward the cart.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack straightened slowly, a habit born of skirmishes where a sudden movement meant a crossbow bolt between the shoulders. She tucked the knife away and spat sideways into the mud.

"Heard him crying, is what you heard." She jerked her head toward the cart. "That's a young voice. Can't be more than sixteen, seventeen. Bad place to be that young, out here." She paused, studying Corvin's face. "But he came with the others, and the others are dead. That's the arithmetic of it."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I swallow, trying to get rid of the taste of blood in my mouth. "So we're the judges now, too?" I finally push myself up, my legs feeling shaky.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack made a sound that might have been a laugh if it had any air behind it. "Judge. Jury. Cleanup crew. Whatever name you want to put on it, the job's the same." She walked past Corvin toward the cart, boots squelching in the churned mud. Halfway there she stopped, looked back.

"Unless you want to pack him up, carry him to the nearest chirurgeon. That'd be three days east, through land we just lost control of last week. He'd probably make it." She shrugged. "Or I can finish it now, clean-like, and we can be gone before the crows find the rest."

She waited, expression unreadable. The crying from the cart hitched and faltered.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "How bad is he?" I ask, and then, because she'll say it anyway: "Bad enough that it's a mercy, or bad enough that it's just easier?"

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack crouched down by the cart wheel, peering underneath. The crying had gone quiet at the sound of her boots, but she could hear the wet rasp of breathing now. She reached in and came back with a hand that was red to the wrist.

"Leg's torn up below the knee," she said, wiping her hand on the grass. "Bone's through the skin. Femur's not hit, or he'd have bled out already, but he's lost a lot. He won't walk on it again, not out here." She paused, tilting her head to listen. "Gut's intact, I think. No exit wound I can see. But he's wet with his own blood and he's been lying in it for a while."

She stood, looking down at Corvin across the cart. "Is it a mercy? Maybe. He's a boy, and he's in a lot of pain, and he's going to die slow if we leave him. Is it easier? I've got a knife and I know where the angle goes. It's not hard. It's just not pleasant." She let out a breath through her nose. "But I'm not going to lie to you and say it's one or the other. Out here, mercy and easier are the same thing. The only question is whether you want to be the one who makes that call, or whether you want me to do it and not talk about it after."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I walk over to the cart and look under it. My stomach turns. "Give me the knife," I say, my voice steadier than I feel. "I'll do it."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack studied him for a long moment, then nodded once. She didn't make a show of it—no solemn handoff, no last-minute warning. She just drew the knife, wiped the blade clean on her thigh, and held it out to him hilt-first.

"Get low, come at him from the head. Don't let him see your face until you're close, and don't let him grab your wrist." She paused, her hand steady. "He's scared. Scared boys do stupid things. If he tries to sit up, put your weight on his chest—not his arm, his chest—and finish it quick. The noise isn't the problem. The noise brings company. It's the hesitation that gets you killed."

She didn't let go of the knife right away. Her eyes met his.

"When you're done, don't look at his face. Not for long. You'll remember it either way, but looking at it makes it worse. Just wipe the blade, stand up, and walk back to me. We'll get moving before it's fully dark."

She released the knife and stepped back, giving him the space to do what needed doing.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I make myself walk over and look at him. "Tell me what I'm looking at," I say to her, because she's seen this before and I haven't, not this close.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack moved to stand beside him, close enough that her voice wouldn't carry past the two of them. She didn't crouch, just looked down at the boy under the cart.

"Leg's the worst of it. You can see where the bone punched through—that pale bit there, that's not cloth, that's him. He's got a flap of skin hanging loose off the shin, but it's not bleeding hard anymore, which means he's got nothing left to lose. His face is grey. That's the blood loss. That's the clock ticking."

She paused, watching him watch the boy.

"He's not looking at your face. He's looking past you, at the sky. That's good. That means he's mostly gone already, just the body's still catching up. You'll want to get down on one knee, keep your weight on his sternum—not enough to crush him, just enough to hold him still if he jerks. Put the knife at the angle I showed you, just behind the jawbone, and push in toward the spine. It's not like the stories. It won't be clean. But it'll be quick."

She let the silence sit for a moment, then added, quieter: "He's not going to thank you. He's not going to say anything at all. But he'll be gone before the sound of it reaches the treeline, and that's the best any of us get out here."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I drop to one knee in the mud, the knife feeling heavy in my hand. I press my other palm against his chest. He doesn't even flinch. "Look away," I tell him, though I know he can't hear me anymore. Then I do what she said.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack heard the sound of it—the wet, final noise that was always the same no matter how many times she heard it. She didn't turn around. She kept her eyes on the treeline, on the shadows getting longer, on the way the light was starting to go amber and gold. She listened to the boy's breathing stop, and then she listened to the silence that followed.

When Corvin stood up, she heard him take a breath—shallow, unsteady. She heard him wipe the blade on the grass, or maybe on his own trouser leg. She didn't watch. Some things you gave a man the privacy of.

She waited until she heard him take a step, then another, and then she turned.

He was walking toward her, the knife hanging loose in his hand. His face was pale under the grime, but his eyes were steady. That was good. That was the thing that mattered. A man who could do what needed doing and still walk straight after—that was a man you could trust to watch your back.

She took the knife from him, wiped it clean on her sleeve, and slid it into the sheath at her hip. She didn't check the edge. She didn't need to.

"Good," she said, and the word came out flatter than she meant it to. She cleared her throat. "You did good. Now we move. The noise carries further than you'd think this time of day."

She turned and started walking, not toward the treeline but along it, angling south. She didn't look back at the cart. She didn't need to. She'd seen it already. She'd seen it a hundred times.

After a few paces she slowed, letting Corvin catch up. She didn't look at him, but her voice was quieter now.

"First one's the worst. They get easier. Not because you stop feeling it, but because you get better at not feeling it." She paused, stepping over a root. "That's not the same as it being all right. But it's what keeps you alive."

She walked on, letting the silence settle between them.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: "Don't clean it up for me," I say. "If I'm going to do this I want to know exactly what a spear does to a man's gut. Tell me straight."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack didn't slow her pace, but she tilted her head slightly, acknowledging the request. She walked a few more steps before she spoke.

"All right. You want straight." She pulled at a strand of tobacco caught between her teeth. "A spear in the gut—depends where. Low down, you've got a chance. High up, you've got less. But neither one's a good way to go."

She gestured vaguely at her own midsection.

"First thing you'll see is the blood. It's not the bright red of an artery hit, it's dark. Sludgy. That's the gut. That's the soup inside you leaking out where it's not supposed to be. The man'll go white in about thirty seconds. Not from blood loss—from shock. His body doesn't know what to do with itself, so it just... stops trying."

She stepped over a fallen branch without looking down.

"He'll be cold. Clammy. He'll probably throw up. If the spear went all the way through, you'll see the exit wound, and that's worse than the entry. The entry's neat. The exit's a hole the size of your fist with stuff hanging out of it that's not supposed to see daylight."

She paused, letting him absorb that.

"He'll be thirsty. Beg for water. Don't give it to him. It'll just come back up, and it'll hurt worse coming up than it did going down. He'll last anywhere from an hour to a day, depending on what got nicked inside. If the bowel's punctured, the rot sets in fast. You'll smell it before he dies. Sweet and sour at the same time. That's the smell of a man turning into a corpse while he's still breathing."

She glanced at him sidelong.

"And you won't be able to do anything for him. Not with what we carry. Not out here. So you either leave him to die slow, or you put a knife in him and move on. And either way, you carry it with you for a while."

She looked ahead again.

"That's what a spear does to a man's gut. You wanted straight. That's it."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I stop walking for a second, the images she's painting stuck in my head. "Thanks," I say, and it sounds stupid but I mean it. "I'd rather know."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack walked a few more paces before she let the corner of her mouth twitch. It wasn't quite a smile, but it was close.

"Most people don't say that," she said. "Most people say 'thanks' like they're trying to get rid of the word. Like they're spitting out something bitter. You sound like you mean it."

She ducked under a low branch, holding it back a moment longer than she needed to, letting it go only when she heard his boots scuff the mud behind her.

"Knowing doesn't make it easier when it happens. It just means you won't waste time being surprised." She paused, rolling her shoulder. "I've seen men die from a splinter that went bad and men walk away from wounds that should've killed them twice over. There's no sense to it. There's no pattern. The only thing you can do is keep moving and don't get attached to the idea that you're going to live."

She glanced back at him, her eyes catching the last of the fading light.

"You did good back there. Not the killing—that's just work. I mean the asking. The wanting to know. That's what keeps you from turning into one of the ones who enjoy it." She looked ahead again. "You're not like that. I can tell. And that's worth something out here. That's worth a lot."

She didn't say anything else. She just kept walking, angling them toward a rise in the treeline where the ground got stony and hard, where they could make camp with a view of the approaches. The silence between them wasn't uncomfortable. It was the silence of a job done and a long road ahead.

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I kneel down and do it, and it isn't clean or quick because I've never done it before. "Stay," I tell her, when she starts to turn away. "Watch it with me and tell me exactly what I'm doing to him — the sound of it, how long he takes, all of it. Don't leave anything out."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stopped walking. She didn't turn around for a long moment, and when she did, her face was unreadable. She studied him in the fading light, the weight of his words settling between them.

"That's not what I've seen men do," she said slowly. "Not the ones who want to forget. Not the ones who want to pretend it didn't happen. You're asking me to hold your eyes open. That's... that's not something I've been asked to do before."

She walked back toward him, not hurrying, and stopped a pace away. She looked at him, then at the cart, then back at him.

"The boy's dead. You already did it. He was gone before you even pulled the blade out—I heard it in his breathing. The sound it makes when the heart stops. You did it right. There was no fumbling. No hesitation." She paused. "You want to know what you did to him? I'll tell you. But I want you to hear me first."

She took a breath, and her voice dropped lower.

"Most men who kill for the first time—they want me to tell them it was quick, that he didn't feel it, that it was clean. They want the lie. They need it to sleep. But you're not asking me to make it easy. You're asking me to make it real. That's braver than putting the knife in. That's the part that's hard."

She held his gaze.

"He was a boy. He was scared. He was bleeding out slow, and you stopped it. What you did was the kindest thing anyone's done for him since his mother held him. But it was still killing, and it's still going to sit in your gut like a stone. You'll feel it when you eat. You'll feel it when you try to sleep. You'll feel it in the silence when there's nothing else to feel."

She reached out, not quite touching his shoulder.

"Tell me you understand that, and I'll tell you everything. Every sound. Every detail. The way his body went slack. The way his hand twitched. The sound the blade made. I'll tell you all of it, and I won't leave anything out. But you'll have to carry it. And you'll have to keep moving. That's the trade."

She let her hand fall.

"So. Do you still want to know?"

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I think I have to. I nod, not trusting my voice to stay steady. "I want the stone," I say, finally. "I want to know how heavy it is."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack held his gaze for a long moment, something shifting behind her eyes—not quite surprise, not quite respect, but a recognition. She gave a single slow nod.

"All right."

She didn't speak right away. She turned and walked to a fallen log, sat down on it with her forearms on her knees, and looked at the ground between her boots. When she spoke, her voice was low and even, the voice she used to point out tripwires and bad ground.

"I was standing about six paces off. I heard it before I saw it. The sound of the blade going in—not the cut, the push. There's a moment where the skin resists, and then it gives. It's not like cutting meat on a board. It's softer. More giving. Like pushing through a ripe piece of fruit, except it's warm and it's alive, and then it isn't."

She looked up at him.

"You went in at the angle I told you. Behind the jawbone, toward the spine. Your hand slipped—I saw it. You didn't have your grip right, and the blade skidded along the bone before it found the gap. It made a sound. A scraping, like a knife on a whetstone, but wet. You'd have felt it in your wrist."

She paused, letting him sit with that.

"He jerked. Not much—he was too far gone for much. But his back arched off the ground and his hands came up. Not to fight you off. Just... a spasm. The body's last attempt to do something. His fingers caught your sleeve. You pulled back—I saw you pull back—but he held on for a second. Not hard. Just the way a child holds on to a hand when they're falling asleep. Then his hand went loose and fell."

She drew a breath.

"You pushed in deeper. You didn't mean to—it was just what happened when he jerked. But you felt it, the way the blade found the way between the bones and the resistance gave way. He made a sound. Not a scream. A breath. A wet, bubbling breath, because there was blood in his throat by then. It came out his mouth and his nose. Not a lot. Just a trickle, dark and thick."

She watched him.

"His eyes were open the whole time. Not looking at you—past you. At the sky. You'd think they'd close, but they don't. They just... go dull. Like the light in them snuffs out. One second there's a person in there, and the next there's just a thing. A body. A piece of meat with a pulse that's still beating a few more times, even though no one's home anymore."

She made a small gesture.

"You held the pressure for a while. You didn't pull the blade out right away. That was good. If you'd pulled it out, there would have been more blood. But you left it in, and the wound closed around it, and the blood pooled in his throat instead. You heard him swallow. That's the last sound he made. A swallow. Then nothing."

She was quiet for a moment.

"When you pulled the blade out, it made a sound like a boot coming out of mud. Wet. Reluctant. There was blood on your hand up to the wrist. You wiped it on the grass, then on your trouser leg. You didn't look at him again. You stood up, and you were shaking—not much, but I saw it. You took a breath like you'd been holding it. Then you walked to me and handed me the knife."

She looked down at her own hands, then back up at him.

"That's what it was. That's what you did. And now you know the weight of it."

She stood up, brushing off the back of her trousers.

"You asked me to tell you straight, and I did. You'll carry it. It won't get lighter, but you'll get stronger. Or you won't. Some men break. Some men just bend." She looked at him, steady. "You didn't break. That's not nothing."

She started walking again, and after a few paces she called back over her shoulder.

"Come on. We've got ground to cover before the moon's up."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I sit back on my heels and I don't get up for a while. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack stopped walking. She didn't turn around at first, just stood there with her back to him, one boot resting on a root, her shoulders rising and falling with a breath she let out slow through her nose. Then she turned, and she walked back. Not all the way—just to the edge of where he sat, close enough that he could see the lines around her eyes in the failing light. She stood over him for a moment, then lowered herself down onto the damp ground, sitting cross-legged in front of him, putting herself at his level. She didn't speak right away. She picked up a twig, snapped it in half, tossed the pieces aside.

"The rest," she said. Not a question. A confirmation. She nodded, mostly to herself. "All right. You want to know what the stone is made of. Not the weight of the act—you've already got that, you can feel it in your gut. You want to know what it does to you after."

She looked at him, and for once she didn't look away. Her voice was low, flat, but not unkind. "Tonight you'll see his face. Not the way you remember it—the grey, the slack jaw. You'll see it the way it was for that one second when you first dropped to your knee and he turned his head toward you. Maybe his eyes focused. Maybe they didn't. But you'll see them anyway. And you'll lie awake and you'll listen to the silence, and the silence will be so loud you'll hear your own heart beating. You'll hear it in your ears, and you'll think it's him. You'll think it's the sound of his heart stopping, over and over."

She picked up another twig, turned it in her fingers. "You'll wash your hands tomorrow, and you'll see the water run clear, and you'll still feel the tackiness under your nails. You'll scrub until the skin's raw, and it won't help, because the feeling isn't on your hands. It's under your skin. You'll reach for something—a waterskin, a strap, a piece of bread—and you'll feel the resistance. The way the blade pushed in. The way it gave. And you'll drop it, and you'll stare at your hand for a long time, and you won't know what you're looking at."

She let the twig fall. "And then, after a while, you'll stop flinching. That's the part nobody tells you. The first few days, it's all you can do not to throw up every time you think about it. But then you'll eat a meal, and you'll taste it. You'll sleep through the night, and you won't dream of him. You'll wake up and for half a breath you won't remember. And then you'll remember, and you'll feel guilty—not because you killed him, but because you forgot, just for a second. Because your body decided to move on, and that feels like betrayal."

She leaned forward slightly. "And then one day, you'll see a man in a similar situation. A boy with a wound, bleeding out, the light going out of his eyes. And you'll feel it in your hand before you even reach for your knife. You'll know exactly what to do. And you'll do it. And it won't be hard. It'll be clean and quick and you'll do it right, and afterward you'll realize you didn't feel anything. Not relief. Not horror. Just... nothing. And that's the real stone, Corvin. Not the killing. The not-feeling. The part of you that can walk away from a body and not look back. That's what you'll carry. That's the weight that doesn't get lighter."

She paused, letting that sit. "You asked for the stone. That's it. The stone is the day you realize you can do this. Not just once, but again. And you will. Because out here, that's what keeps you alive. But every time you do it, a little piece of you goes quiet. And after enough times, you start to wonder if there's anything left that isn't quiet. That's what it costs. That's the weight."

She looked at him, and her expression softened, just a fraction. "You're not there yet. You're shaking. You're sitting in the mud with a dead boy's blood on your hands, and you're shaking. That's good. That means it's real. That means you're still you. But you wanted to know what the rest is. The rest is the day you stop shaking. And you'll hate yourself for it, and you'll be grateful for it, and you'll never know which one is true. That's the stone. You can't put it down. You just learn to carry it."

She stood up, brushed the dirt off her trousers, and held out her hand to him. "Now get up. We've got ground to cover. And you're going to want to be moving when the moon comes up, because the night's going to be cold, and you've got nothing to keep you warm but a dead boy's ghost and the memory of what his throat felt like when the light went out." She waited, hand extended, not pushing, not pulling. "That's the rest. All of it. Now you know. So get up, and we'll go."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I take her hand and let her pull me up. My fingers are cold. "Yeah," I say, and my voice sounds strange to me. "Let's go."

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack heard the strange note in his voice and it stopped her mid-turn. She stood there, half-turned away, and let out a breath that wasn't quite a sigh. Then she looked back at him, and for a moment her face was open in a way it rarely was—not soft, but not hard either. Just a face that had seen too much and was still willing to look.

"Yeah," she said, and the word came out quieter than she meant it to. "That's the voice. The one that doesn't sound like yours. It'll do that for a while." She paused, her eyes scanning his face in the failing light. "You'll hear it when you talk, and you'll think, 'That's not me,' and you'll be right. It's not. It's the part of you that's still trying to make sense of what you did. It's the part that's still back there, kneeling in the mud, wondering how you got here."

She took a step back toward him, not close enough to crowd him, but close enough that her voice didn't have to carry. "It'll get quieter. Not because it goes away, but because you'll get used to it. And one day you'll hear yourself say something, and you won't recognize the voice, and you'll realize that's the one that's going to keep you alive." She let that settle. "The strange one, I mean. The one that doesn't sound like you. It's the one that keeps you from getting comfortable. It's the one that makes you check your back and your corners and the shadows under the cart. It's the one that's going to keep you breathing."

She turned and started walking again, but slower this time, letting him catch up on his own. "Now come on. We've got a cold night ahead and a hard ground to sleep on. And if you're lucky, you'll be too tired to dream." She didn't look back. "That's the best you can hope for tonight."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I fall into step beside her, my boots making less noise than I expect. "You didn't have to sit with me like that," I say, because I can't think of anything else.

dialogue.name: Wrack
dialogue.content:
Wrack walked a few more paces before she answered, and when she did, she didn't turn around. "I know I didn't." She stepped over a loose stone, nudged it aside with her boot. "But you'd have sat there all night, otherwise. And I'm too old to be sleeping with one eye open because my new partner decided to have his first crisis in the middle of bandit country."

She let the words hang there for a moment, then stopped. She turned, just enough to look at him over her shoulder. "Also, someone had to tell you the truth about it. Most people don't get that. They get the lie—the 'it gets easier' or the 'you did what you had to'—and then they spend the next ten years wondering why the lie doesn't fit right."

She looked at him for a long moment, her face half in shadow. "You asked me not to leave anything out. That's rare. And it's worth sitting in the mud for."

She turned back and started walking again, her boots finding the familiar rhythm of the trail. "Don't make a habit of it, though. I'm not in the business of holding hands." A pause. "But if you need to stop again, I'll stop with you. Just don't tell the others—I've got a reputation to keep."

dialogue.name: Corvin
dialogue.content: I let out a sound that’s almost a laugh. "Wouldn't dream of it." The silence stretches between us, not heavy, just there. "Thanks, Wrack."
